strengths: Comprehensive and well-designed empirical study spanning three modeling paradigms (text-based with acoustic features, a novel audio-only architecture AudioSeg, and MLLMs), providing a broad and useful comparison for an underexplored task.

The formalization of evaluation protocols (R1, H1, H2/H3, T1, T2) is a genuine methodological contribution: it clearly articulates the domain mismatch between text-space and time-space evaluation and offers concrete, reproducible procedures (including oracle segmentation analysis) that quantify the discretization loss inherent to transcript-based metrics.

The empirical findings are interesting and non-trivial: pause duration drives most of the gain from acoustic features, learned audio representations (especially Whisper-derived) outperform text-only models, and MLLMs show marked context-length/instruction-following limitations that are carefully diagnosed via a detailed failure analysis (missing transcripts, generation loops, WER of generated transcripts).

Extensive ablations and stratified analyses (by duration, speaker regime, audio encoder, feature category, evaluation protocol) add robustness and nuance to the claims, going beyond aggregate metrics.

The paper is transparent about limitations (single dataset, English-only, no fine-tuning of larger MLLMs) and plans to release code, AudioSeg, and new annotations (duration/speaker regimes, ASR variants), which supports reproducibility and future work.
Clear writing and logical organization, with the evaluation protocol section building carefully from text-space to time-space formulations.
weaknesses: All experiments rely on a single dataset (YTSeg), which is English-only and drawn from YouTube; generalizability to other domains (podcasts, lectures, meetings) or languages is unverified despite the paper's framing as addressing chaptering broadly.

The comparison between AudioSeg and text-based models is somewhat confounded: AudioSeg's strong performance is largely attributed to using a Whisper Large encoder pretrained on similar data, while other encoders (HuBERT, PEA-Frame) perform much worse; the paper acknowledges but does not fully control for this domain-match confound, making the claim 'audio is superior to text' less clean than presented.

MLLM evaluation is restricted to videos <30 minutes due to context limitations, which is reasonable but means the paper's practical claims about MLLM viability are only partial and the reported cross-model comparisons (Table 4 vs Table 7) are not on identical test subsets, complicating direct comparison.

The magnitude of some effects (e.g., pause duration contributing nearly all gains from audio features, only 2-3 F1 point differences in several ablations) raises questions about statistical significance; no significance testing or variance/error bars are reported across runs, limiting confidence in some fine-grained claims (e.g., single feature category comparisons in Table 5).

The novelty of AudioSeg's architecture itself is somewhat incremental (a fairly standard hierarchical chunk-window-document transformer over frozen encoder features), with the paper's main contribution more in the systematic comparison and evaluation formalization than in a fundamentally new modeling technique.

Some evaluation protocol contributions (e.g., collar-based/continuous-time evaluation and time-chunk protocols) build on established ideas from diarization/sound event detection and prior topic segmentation work (Guinaudeau et al. 2010), so the degree of protocol novelty is moderate despite being described as newly 'formalized' and 'systemized' for this task.
The paper does not report human evaluation or qualitative validation of chapter title quality for the MLLM setting, despite title generation being part of the task motivation stated in Section 3.4.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored problem: most prior work treats audio chaptering as a pure text segmentation task; the paper explicitly examines the role of audio, ASR quality, and transcript-free evaluation.

The evaluation protocol taxonomy (R1, H1, H2/H3, T1, T2) is a useful conceptual contribution, clearly articulating the mismatch between discrete text-space and continuous time-space chapter evaluation, and the oracle-segmentation analysis (Table A5) nicely quantifies the lossiness of transcript-based protocols.

Broad, thorough experimental sweep across text-based models, hand-crafted acoustic features, multiple audio encoders for AudioSeg, and several MLLM inference strategies (zero-shot, ICL, chunking, self-cascade, LoRA), with useful stratified analyses by duration and speaker regime.

Reasonable reproducibility support: hyperparameters, prompts, and dataset annotation procedures (duration/speaker regimes, ASR variants) are documented in appendices, and the authors commit to releasing code, AudioSeg, and annotations.
Interesting ablations, e.g., the DeepFilterNet non-speech-cue ablation and the pause-duration feature analysis, that support some causal claims about what acoustic information helps.
weaknesses: The central claim that audio-only segmentation is 'not only viable but superior' to text-based approaches is confounded: the best AudioSeg variant uses Whisper Large, a much larger and more heavily pretrained encoder (trained implicitly for ASR on massive multilingual/YouTube-like data) than the small MiniLM sentence encoder used in the text baseline. The comparison is therefore not clearly isolating modality (audio vs. text) from encoder scale/pretraining data, which is a serious threat to the validity of the paper's headline finding, and the paper only partially acknowledges this (domain-match speculation) without controlling for it (e.g., no text baseline using large pretrained LM embeddings of comparable scale).

The superiority of AudioSeg is itself duration-limited: for videos beyond ~30 minutes, text-based models are competitive or better than AudioSeg (Table A3), yet the abstract and conclusion state a much stronger, less qualified claim ('AudioSeg substantially outperforms text-based approaches'), which risks overstating the generality of the result.

No statistical significance testing or variance/confidence intervals are reported anywhere despite many close comparisons (e.g., 1-3 point F1 differences between MiniSeg transcript variants, or between individual acoustic feature categories), making it hard to assess whether the many fine-grained empirical claims (e.g., 'pitch and speaking rate show no improvement') are robust rather than noise.

MLLM evaluation is restricted to videos under 30 minutes due to context limitations, which is a reasonable practical constraint but substantially limits the generality of conclusions about MLLM capability on the full duration distribution used elsewhere in the paper, creating an inconsistent basis for comparison across models.

Despite formalizing six evaluation protocols, only T1 (discrete time) is actually used for the main comparative results; T2 (continuous-time) is proposed but never empirically applied, making part of the methodological contribution more expository than empirically validated.

The core AudioSeg architecture (frozen encoder + local transformer + RoFormer document encoder) is a relatively standard combination of existing components; the novelty lies mainly in the empirical study/benchmarking framing rather than in a new modeling technique.

Reliance on a single English-only dataset (YTSeg) for all findings, combined with the reliance on automatic pipelines (Whisper ASR, TitaNet diarization) to produce reference annotations used for both training and evaluation, introduces additional annotation noise that is not analyzed or propagated into uncertainty estimates for downstream conclusions.

strengths: Comprehensive systematic comparison across three modeling paradigms (text-based with/without acoustic features, novel audio-only AudioSeg, and MLLMs), providing one of the most thorough empirical studies of audio chaptering to date.

Careful and useful formalization of evaluation protocols (R1, H1, H2/H3, T1, T2) that clearly articulates and demonstrates (via oracle segmentation and protocol-comparison experiments) the real problem of transcript-dependent metrics being non-comparable across ASR qualities -- a genuine and underappreciated methodological issue for the field.

Rich empirical analyses (duration regime, speaker regime, ASR quality, non-speech cue ablation with DeepFilterNet) that go beyond aggregate numbers and yield actionable, non-obvious findings (e.g., pause duration drives most acoustic gains; ASR WER does not directly predict segmentation quality; speaker features help specifically in multi-speaker content).

Substantial engineering and experimental effort: multiple audio encoders for AudioSeg, multiple MLLM inference strategies (zero-shot, ICL, chunking, self-cascaded, LoRA), and detailed failure-mode analysis of MLLM outputs (Table A2), which is a valuable diagnostic contribution.

Good reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, prompts, feature-extraction methodology, and forced-alignment procedures are provided in appendices, and the authors commit to releasing code, AudioSeg, and dataset annotations (duration/speaker regimes, ASR transcripts).

The dataset augmentation (duration/speaker regime labels, two ASR transcript variants) is a useful resource contribution on top of YTSeg that could benefit future work even independent of the modeling contributions.
weaknesses: No statistical significance testing or variance estimates (e.g., multiple seeds) are reported for the main results tables, making it hard to assess whether some of the reported differences (e.g., MiniSeg ASR_T vs ASR_L, or small F1 gains from individual audio features) are robust rather than noise.

The comparison between AudioSeg (built on large pretrained encoders such as Whisper Large) and text-based MiniSeg (built on MiniLM) is not controlled for model/encoder capacity or pretraining data scale, so the claim that audio representations are intrinsically superior to text is confounded with encoder size and domain match (the paper itself notes Whisper's YouTube-similar pretraining data as a likely contributor, but does not disentangle this further).

All experiments are on a single, English-only dataset (YTSeg); while acknowledged as a limitation and justified by the lack of alternatives, this constrains the generalizability of the specific empirical conclusions (e.g., about pause features or duration effects) to this data distribution.

MLLM experiments are restricted to videos <30 minutes due to context limitations, and LoRA fine-tuning was only performed on the smaller Qwen2.5-Omni due to compute constraints, leaving the paper's conclusions about MLLM "promise" and context limitations somewhat provisional and not fully explored for the strongest model.

The 6-second chunk size for the primary T1 protocol, while motivated by average sentence length, is a somewhat ad hoc choice presented without sensitivity analysis across different chunk granularities, which could affect the reported cross-model rankings.

Evaluation relies entirely on automatic segmentation metrics (F1, B, Pk); no human evaluation of chapter quality or usefulness is conducted, which would strengthen claims about practical relevance of the different approaches, especially given known limitations/quirks of Pk and boundary-similarity metrics.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely underexplored and practically relevant task (audio chaptering) with a clear articulation of the transcript-centric bias in prior work, motivating both new modeling and new evaluation.

Contributes on three fronts simultaneously — modeling (AudioSeg, feature-augmented MiniSeg, MLLM prompting variants), empirical analysis (ASR robustness, feature ablations, duration/speaker/domain effects), and evaluation methodology (formalization of R1/H1/H2/H3/T1/T2 protocols) — which together constitute a substantial and coherent body of work rather than a single narrow claim.

Extensive experimentation: multiple audio encoders, multiple ASR qualities, multiple MLLM prompting/adaptation strategies (zero-shot, ICL, chunking, self-cascade, LoRA), stratified analyses by duration and speaker regime, and cross-domain validation on AMI.

Useful negative/nuanced findings (e.g., WER does not straightforwardly predict segmentation performance; MLLMs bottlenecked by temporal grounding rather than topic detection; non-speech cues such as music explain some AudioSeg gains) that provide actionable insight for future work.

Care taken to validate the proposed time-space evaluation protocol against text-space protocols and across granularities, supporting the reproducibility and soundness of the transcript-invariant evaluation contribution.
Practical artifacts released (toolkit, AudioSeg, augmented YTSeg annotations for duration/speaker/ASR variants), aiding reproducibility and follow-up research.
weaknesses: The central claim that audio-only AudioSeg 'substantially outperforms' text-based models is potentially confounded: the best AudioSeg variant uses a Whisper-Large encoder, which itself is trained on ASR (i.e., implicitly encodes linguistic/transcript-like information) and is far larger/more heavily pretrained than the MiniLM+RoFormer text stack; the paper does not fully disentangle whether gains stem from 'audio beyond transcripts' or simply from stronger/larger pretrained representations.

Reliance on a single primary dataset (YTSeg) for nearly all main findings; the AMI cross-domain check uses only 16 test meetings (4 for the <30 min subset), which is too small to strongly support generalization claims stated in the conclusion.
English-only data limits claims about broader applicability, acknowledged but not mitigated.

MLLM results (segmentation, temporal grounding, title generation) are restricted to videos <30 minutes due to context limits, which is a substantial coverage gap given that over half of the dataset (duration ≥30 min) is excluded from these comparisons, yet the abstract/conclusion make general statements about MLLM promise.

No statistical significance testing or variance/error bars are reported for the many pairwise comparisons (feature ablations, encoder comparisons, protocol comparisons), making it hard to assess whether reported differences (e.g., +0.67 F1 for speaker features overall) are robust or within noise.

The evaluation protocol suite (R1, H1, H2, H3, T1, T2) is elaborate; while useful, its practical necessity versus simpler alternatives is not strongly justified beyond showing ranking consistency, and some hybrid protocols (H2/H3) are introduced but relatively underexplored in the main results.
Some findings appear dataset/domain-specific (e.g., pause duration dominating acoustic gains may reflect YouTube editing conventions) but are generalized in the conclusion without sufficient caveat.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical study spanning three modeling paradigms (text-based+features, novel audio-only AudioSeg, MLLMs) with consistent, well-documented experimental protocols across all of them.

The formalization of evaluation protocols (R1, H1, H2/H3, T1, T2) addresses a genuine and previously under-articulated methodological gap in the field — the paper clearly demonstrates via oracle segmentation (F1≈73-81%) that transcript-based text-space evaluation is inherently lossy, and shows T1/T2 give consistent, transcript-invariant rankings.

AudioSeg is a reasonably novel and effective architecture; the finding that a purely audio-based model with a frozen Whisper encoder outperforms strong text-based baselines is a substantive and non-obvious empirical result.

Extensive supporting analyses: pause-duration ablation, speaker-regime stratification, duration stratification, granularity-sensitivity checks, MLLM failure-mode taxonomy, and cross-domain validation on AMI, all of which strengthen the credibility and interpretability of the main claims.
Good reproducibility effort: detailed hyperparameters, prompts, feature-extraction methodology, and a stated intention to release code, annotations, and the AudioSeg model/toolkit.
Honest, specific limitations section (single primary dataset, English-only, inability to fine-tune larger MLLMs) rather than vague boilerplate.
weaknesses: Almost all quantitative claims rely on a single primary dataset (YTSeg); the only cross-domain check (AMI) uses extremely small val/test splits (9/4 and 16/16 meetings), which is too small to be statistically convincing evidence of generalization despite being described as validating the 'main conclusions'.

No confidence intervals, variance across seeds/runs, or significance testing are reported anywhere in the main results (e.g., Table 4, 5, 6, 7), making it hard to assess whether reported differences (e.g., +0.67 F1 from speaker features, or small gaps between MiniSeg ASR variants) are meaningful or noise.

The central claim that 'audio is superior to text' rests heavily on AudioSeg with a Whisper-Large encoder, which is itself trained on massive weakly-supervised ASR data (plausibly including YouTube-like audio); the paper acknowledges possible domain-match confounds but does not control for this, weakening the causal interpretation that 'learned audio representations capture structural cues beyond transcripts' versus 'Whisper encoder is simply a stronger/better-matched feature extractor'.

Comparisons across MLLMs (Qwen2.5-Omni vs Qwen3-Omni) conflate model capability differences with prompting-strategy differences (e.g., LoRA only applied to Qwen2.5-Omni, not Qwen3-Omni, due to compute constraints), which limits clean attribution of gains to strategy vs. underlying model quality.
Title-quality evaluation relies solely on automatic metrics (BERTScore, ROUGE-L) without any human evaluation, which is a known weakness for assessing generative quality of short titles.

The novelty of the AudioSeg architecture itself is somewhat incremental, combining a frozen pretrained encoder, a local segment transformer, and a RoFormer document encoder — largely a recombination of existing components rather than a fundamentally new modeling idea; the main contribution is empirical rather than architectural.

Some evaluation-protocol contributions (T2 collar-based scoring) are explicitly noted by the authors to be adaptations of existing practice from sound event detection/diarization rather than new formulations, slightly limiting the novelty claim of 'systematizing' evaluation.

strengths: Provides a genuinely useful formalization of audio-chaptering evaluation protocols (R1, H1, H2/H3, T1, T2), clearly diagnosing a real methodological problem (transcript-dependent metrics being non-comparable across ASR systems) and proposing concrete, well-motivated remedies (time-space evaluation).

Broad and carefully designed experimental matrix: text-only baselines, hand-crafted acoustic feature ablations, a new audio-only architecture (AudioSeg) with six different pretrained encoders, and multiple MLLM prompting/adaptation strategies (zero-shot, ICL, chunking, self-cascade, LoRA), which together substantiate the paper's central claims rather than relying on a single comparison.

Strong empirical support for key claims: oracle segmentation analysis quantifies discretization loss (73-81% ceiling) motivating time-based protocols; DeepFilterNet ablation causally verifies that non-speech acoustic cues (not just semantic leakage) drive AudioSeg's gains; granularity-sensitivity checks (T1 at multiple chunk sizes, T2 continuous) show ranking consistency, adding robustness to the reported findings.

Fine-grained analyses (duration regime, speaker regime, cross-domain AMI validation) go beyond aggregate metrics and reveal non-obvious, actionable findings (e.g., speaker features specifically help multi-speaker content; text-based models regain competitiveness on very long videos due to training data sparsity).

Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameters, prompts, feature-extraction methodology, and stated release of an evaluation toolkit, AudioSeg code, and new YTSeg annotations (duration/speaker regimes, ASR transcript variants).
weaknesses: The dataset scope is narrow: primary conclusions rest on a single dataset (YTSeg, English-only YouTube videos) and the paper leans on averages/single-run numbers throughout the main results tables (e.g., Tables 4-7) without confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests, which limits confidence in fine-grained comparisons (e.g., small F1 deltas between MiniSeg variants trained on ASR_T vs ASR_L).

AMI is used as the only out-of-domain validation, but it is small-scale (16 test meetings) and the paper does not report whether AudioSeg/MiniSeg differences on AMI are stable across seeds or splits, weakening the generalization claim beyond YTSeg-style YouTube chaptering.

The central claim that 'transcript-free segmentation is superior' rests heavily on Whisper-Large-based AudioSeg, which the authors themselves note likely benefits from domain match to YouTube-style audio (its pretraining data) and implicit ASR-derived linguistic structure; this potential confound is acknowledged only briefly and not further disentangled (e.g., no controlled comparison isolating domain-match effects from 'audio provides unique information').

MLLM evaluation is restricted to a single model family (Qwen2.5/3-Omni) and to short/medium-duration audio (<30 min) due to context constraints, limiting how strongly the MLLM-related conclusions (e.g., about instruction-following and temporal grounding) generalize to other MLLMs or longer content.

Some of the paper's explanatory narratives for observed patterns (e.g., why ASR_L underperforms ASR_T despite lower WER, or why AudioSeg's advantage disappears for very long videos) are attributed post-hoc to plausible but untested hypotheses (granularity mismatch, training-data sparsity) rather than being verified with additional targeted experiments.
